title: Statistical Power & Effect Size

references.label: General microbiology/quantitative methods references (ASM, FDA BAM, CLSI)

summary: Statistical power is the probability that a study will detect a real effect if one truly exists, given its sample size and the size of the effect itself; effect size is a measure of how large that real difference actually is, independent of sample size.
explanation: A study with too few replicates (low power) can easily fail to detect a real, meaningful biological effect, producing a 'no significant difference' result that reflects insufficient sample size rather than a true absence of effect. Effect size matters alongside power because a very large sample can make even a tiny, practically meaningless difference statistically significant, while a small sample can miss even a substantial, practically important difference. Planning sample size in advance (a power analysis), using an expected or pilot-derived effect size, is the standard way to avoid both an underpowered study that misses real effects and an unnecessarily large study that wastes resources.

comparison.example: Too few replicates to reliably detect a real effect, risking a false 'no difference' conclusion
A very large sample size making a tiny, biologically unimportant difference reach statistical significance

commonMisconceptions: Treating 'not statistically significant' as proof there is no real effect, without considering whether the study had enough power to detect one.
Equating statistical significance with practical or biological importance — the two are related but distinct.
